interactions.label: The majority of biomedical waste generated in Indian hospitals is classified as

params.question: The majority of biomedical waste generated in Indian hospitals is classified as infectious or hazardous.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Actually, only 15–20% of biomedical waste is classified as infectious or hazardous. The bulk — 80 to 85% — is general waste. This is precisely why segregation at the point of generation is so critical: it keeps the larger general stream uncontaminated.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Only 15–20% of the roughly 600 tonnes of biomedical waste generated daily in India is infectious or hazardous. The remaining 80–85% is general waste that, if properly segregated, can safely enter the municipal waste stream.

interactions.label: Which of the following best explains why syringes are placed in the red bag only

params.question: Which of the following best explains why syringes are placed in the red bag only after the needle has been removed?

answers.text: Needles blunt during autoclaving and become harder to shred

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Autoclaving does not significantly affect needle sharpness. The real reason is that the needle and barrel belong to different waste streams — sharps (white container) and recyclable plastics (red bag) — each with its own mandated treatment.

answers.text: The plastic barrel is a recyclable material requiring autoclaving, while the needle is a sharp requiring a separate treatment pathway

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Exactly. The plastic barrel can be autoclaved, shredded, and recycled (red bag stream), whereas the sharp needle must go into a puncture-proof white container. Separating the two ensures each component follows its correct treatment pathway.

answers.text: Red bags are not puncture-proof, so needles would tear them during transport

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While red bags are indeed not puncture-proof, the fundamental reason is that needles and plastic barrels belong to different waste categories with different treatment methods — sharps vs. recyclable plastics.

answers.text: Needles contain heavy metals that contaminate the plastic recycling process

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Standard medical needles do not contain heavy metals. The separation is needed because the needle (a sharp) and the barrel (a recyclable plastic) require different, category-specific treatment pathways.

overallFeedback.feedback: The plastic barrel is recyclable (red bag → autoclaving → shredding → recycling), while the needle is a sharp (white container → separate treatment). Each waste category has its own mandated pathway under the BMW Rules 2016.
Well done. Understanding why waste components are separated — different materials, different treatment pathways — is key to following the four-category system correctly.

interactions.label: Which treatment method is appropriate for contaminated recyclable plastics colle

params.question: Which treatment method is appropriate for contaminated recyclable plastics collected in the red bag?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incineration is reserved for yellow-bag waste — anatomical, cytotoxic, and pharmaceutical waste. Incinerating recyclable plastics would destroy material that can be safely recycled after proper disinfection.
Deep burial is an option only for remote facilities without access to other treatment methods, and is typically used for anatomical waste. Recyclable plastics need autoclaving, not burial.
Correct. Red-bag plastics are autoclaved at 121°C for 30–60 minutes to eliminate pathogens, then shredded and sent for recycling. This preserves the material while ensuring safety.
Encapsulation is specifically for sharps containers once three-quarters full — the sharps are sealed in a solidifying agent before final disposal. Recyclable plastics in red bags require autoclaving.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct treatment for red-bag recyclable plastics is autoclaving at 121°C for 30–60 minutes, followed by shredding and recycling. The BMW Rules 2016 mandate treatment method by waste category, not facility preference.
Correct. Autoclaving effectively sterilises contaminated plastics while preserving them for recycling — a key advantage over incineration for this waste category.

interactions.label: What is the primary purpose of requiring bar-coded labels on biomedical waste ba

params.question: What is the primary purpose of requiring bar-coded labels on biomedical waste bags sent for treatment?

answers.text: To record the weight of each bag for billing the treatment facility

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While waste quantities are logged, bar-coded labels serve a broader purpose: creating a complete tracking trail from generation to final disposal, enabling accountability at every stage of the waste chain.

answers.text: To create a tracking trail from the point of waste generation to its final disposal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The BMW Rules 2016 introduced bar-coded labelling so that every waste bag can be traced from the ward where it was generated, through transport, to its final treatment and disposal — ensuring accountability and enabling audit if things go wrong.

answers.text: To identify which staff member sealed each individual bag

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Staff identification may be part of facility records, but bar-coded labels are designed for a broader purpose — tracking the waste bag through the entire chain from generation to treatment and final disposal.

answers.text: To ensure that the waste is treated within 24 hours of generation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 24-hour reporting requirement applies to equipment failures, not to waste bag processing. Bar-coded labels serve as a tracking mechanism creating an end-to-end trail from generation to disposal.

overallFeedback.feedback: Bar-coded labels create a tracking trail from the point of waste generation all the way to final disposal. This end-to-end traceability is a key monitoring tool under the BMW Rules 2016.
Correct. Bar-coded labels create an auditable chain of custody — from generation to disposal — so that any lapse in handling can be traced back to its source.

interactions.label: During wound care, you generate blood-soaked gauze. Into which container should

params.question: During wound care, you generate blood-soaked gauze. Into which container should it be discarded?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Red bags are for recyclable plastics like IV tubing and catheters. Blood-soaked gauze is soiled, non-recyclable material — it cannot be autoclaved and recycled like plastics can.

Correct. Blood-soaked gauze is soiled, non-recyclable waste. It goes into the yellow bag for incineration. The narration specifically contrasts this with the IV cannula scenario — the plastic catheter (recyclable) goes to red, but soiled dressings go to yellow.
White containers are reserved for sharps — needles, blades, and lancets. Gauze is not a sharp and poses no puncture risk; it belongs in the yellow bag as soiled waste.
Blue boxes are for glassware and metallic implants that can be disinfected and sent to an authorised recycler. Blood-soaked gauze is soiled, non-recyclable waste — it belongs in the yellow bag.

overallFeedback.feedback: Blood-soaked gauze is soiled, non-recyclable waste — it belongs in the yellow bag for incineration. Unlike plastic items such as IV tubing (red bag), gauze cannot be autoclaved and recycled.

Well done. Blood-soaked gauze is soiled, non-recyclable waste that goes into the yellow bag — a common scenario that tests whether you can distinguish soiled dressings (yellow) from recyclable plastics (red).
